paragraphs.text: How pantry users first learned about the food pantry and the pathways through which they discovered available services.

Description: Educational institutions serve as trusted intermediaries connecting families to food assistance, with schools acting as information hubs through counselors, teachers, and school-home communications.

Description: Family members including extended family networks play a critical role in pantry discovery, often based on their own prior experience with food assistance or awareness of family members' needs.
"My grandmother told me about the pantry"
"Fiance does the online ordering and likes the different options available but go to Helping Place to supplement missing food items"

Description: Personal friendships serve as informal information channels, with friends sharing not only pantry location but also operational details like choice-based selection models that reduce stigma.
"Heard about pantry for first time through their Friend"
"Friend shared pantry allows choosing own items"
Description: Digital tools enable self-directed pantry discovery, with users finding information through websites, search engines, and mapping applications without relying on interpersonal referrals.
"Saw pantry location via online map or coordinates"

Description: Healthcare facilities and other service organizations act as critical touchpoints for pantry referrals, identifying food insecurity during service interactions and directing clients to nearby resources.
"Went to pantry because it was recommended"
"From healthcare service across the road (Healthcare service is a critical touchpoint that SECS doesn't expose much about it)"
"Noticed pantry during clinic (across the street) visit"
Description: Some referral sources are ambiguous or represent overlapping social networks that blur boundaries between family and friends.

The "Concentric Model" of Trust: Discovery is primarily relational (Word of mouth), not informational. The most common pathways are Family and Friends (Inner Circle), followed by Schools (Trusted Institutions). Digital discovery is secondary.
Proximity Discovery: The mention of "noticed... across the street" confirms that physical visibility remains a key discovery factor, especially when paired with trusted locations like clinics.
What motivates users to visit or continue to visit the pantry?
Definition: Motivations driven by the physical location of the pantry relative to the user’s daily life, highlighting the relationship between distance, time, and cost.
"Pickup kids and pickup food from pantry on the way"
"Family has lived in area for generations"
"Pantry is in convenient location right out the highway"
"Being closer or not influences continued use of the service"
Code: Generational Ties (e.g., family has lived in the neighborhood for generations, familiarity with the area)
Definition: The specific economic context of the hunger, ranging from temporary student needs to chronic underemployment.
"Extra money saved on groceries help with clothing the large family"
"They were giving away food for low income families"
Transitional Support (e.g., goal-based assistance to reach next life stage)
"They were studying so they couldn't work so needed food assistance"
Money saved on groceries allows spending on clothing/bills, acting as a safety net)
"Economy is bad," inflation, sudden financial shifts
Definition: The pantry functioning as a social hub where users engage in mutual aid and reciprocity.
Helping others who cannot physically go to the pantry
Resource Redistribution (e.g., users share ingredients with neighbors
Definition: Psychological motivators and barriers related to self-reliance and the dignity of the user.
"Only you can take care of you,"

1. The "Working Hungry" Phenomenon: The data challenges the stigma that pantry users are unemployed. A significant motivation is strategic financial management for the "working hungry"—those who have jobs (or are students) but face an income gap. For these users, the pantry is a tool to offset grocery costs so they can afford other essentials like clothing or bills.
SECS requires a targeted strategy to support users identified as “working hungry” in accessing career services.

2. Proximity is an Economic Factor, Not Just Convenience: While convenience is mentioned, the underlying driver for proximity is economic. "Short drive saves gas" indicates that if a pantry is too far, the cost of fuel negates the value of food aid. This validates the project's focus on mobility; if the "last mile" is too expensive, the service becomes inaccessible.
3. Invisible Infrastructure: Users are actively "helping others who cannot go," creating an invisible layer of community delivery.

4. Autonomy as a Barrier and a Motivator: The "Autonomy" notes (e.g., "only you can take care of you") suggest psychological tension. While users are motivated by a desire to stabilize their lives, this strong sense of self-reliance may also act as a barrier to accepting "help" until it is absolutely necessary. It may drive them to view the pantry as a temporary  steppingstone rather than a "goal-based" support.

3. Transportation & Mobility
How do pantry users access the pantry/services?
Definition: The specific methods users employ to reach the pantry, highlighting a strong reliance on private vehicles rather than public infrastructure alone.
2 hour walk to access other stores
Definition: Financial constraints that limit the usability of available transportation methods, specifically regarding fuel and transit fares.
Challenges arise from not always having gas available
having money for gas makes trips more manageable
Public transportation is not affordable to be used whenever needed
Definition: Physical challenges related to the "last mile" of the pantry experience, specifically the capacity to move goods and navigate the environment.
Carrying bags while walking back home is challenging
Seniors with mobility issues are unable to get out
getting items to those who cannot come
Other Evidence: Bad weather/Cold weather as a barrier
Other Evidence:  Some pantries require users to be onsite for pick-up, Zip code needed
Definition: External systemic issues related to the built environment that impede access.
Other Evidence: Bus stop is far from destination
Service Isolation (e.g., Transportation barrier as a reason to not use other services/extra services)

1. The "Gas Gap" vs. Car Ownership: A critical distinction in the data is that owning a car does not equal reliable access. "Financial Barriers" explicitly mention "not having gas all the time". This suggests that for many users, the vehicle exists as an asset, but the operating cost (fuel) is the actual obstacle. This is a "working poverty" indicator consistent with Theme 1.

2. The "Last Mile" Problem (Carrying Capacity): The data highlights a specific logistical failure in the current model: "Can't carry groceries far". This indicates that even if a user can reach the pantry (by bus or walking), the return trip is physically unmanageable due to the weight of the goods. This validates the need for delivery or AV intervention for the "last mile.”
To what extent do pantry users know about the services offered by SECs, and are they interested in using them?  (Patterns for the dynamics between different types of pantry users)
Description: Users are unaware that pantries offer services beyond food distribution, representing a fundamental information gap in how pantries are perceived and how services are communicated.
Description: Complete absence of knowledge about non-food services, often because users view pantries solely as emergency food providers.
"Not Heard about other SEC services" (multiple instances)
"Not aware of other pantry services" (multiple instances)
"Was not aware of pantries and services when not in need"
Description: Once aware that services exist, users express curiosity and openness to explore offerings, indicating that awareness itself is a primary barrier rather than lack of interest.
Sub-theme 4.2: Not Interested / No Perceived Need
Description: Users are aware services exist but do not see relevance to their current situation, revealing misalignment between service offerings and perceived needs.
"Not interested in knowing more about the services"
"Not interested in other services right now"
"Feels pantry cannot help them with working toward their goal"

Description: Users explicitly reject specific service categories (education, financial guidance, job coaching), suggesting these offerings may not match their current priorities or that messaging hasn't demonstrated relevance.
Description: Users know services exist but have not engaged, representing a critical gap between awareness and action that practical, psychological, or systemic barriers create.
"Aware of other pantry services beyond food pickup, like job coaching or financial or education support"
"Neighbor have heard of all the other services"
"Aware that pantry supports housing, finances, and medical needs"
"Heard about non-food services but hasn't received them personally"

Description: Time scarcity—particularly for working families juggling multiple jobs—prevents service engagement even when interest exists, revealing structural barriers that informational strategies alone cannot address.
"Lack of time is barrier to using other programs" (multiple instances)
"Aware of other pantry services at SEC but already works many jobs and does not have time to look into these services"
Sub-theme 4.4: Need Clear Information / Pathway Uncertainty
Description: Users want to engage but lack concrete details about how services work, what benefits they provide, how to start, or whether they qualify—creating hesitation and preventing action.
"Feels uncertain about how pantry can help more"
"No clear path to guide them further to the services"
"Unsure why they would not use job resources"
"Motivated to learn if pantry was free"
"Heard of services but...Don't know how to start"
Description: When information exists, it is often unclear, outdated, incomplete, or uses jargon that obscures rather than clarifies what services offer.
"Need more communication of services, need more information of services"
"Unclarity of the meaning of career coaching/education"
"Accurate information needed of dates and times"
Description: Users who have engaged with non-food services, providing insight into what actual service experiences look like and where follow-through may break down.
"SECS offers clothing services as one of the other services where they provide new clothes"
"Has attended english classes and taken financial counseling as a part of other services"
"Tried counseling service but received no follow-up"
Sub-theme 4.6: First-Time Pantry Experience / First Impressions

Description: Initial interactions with the pantry shape long-term engagement patterns, with first impressions determining whether users feel welcome, understood, and willing to explore additional services.

Description: Factors that influence whether users feel safe, heard, and supported when considering service engagement—highlighting the role of relationships, reliability, and emotional safety in service uptake.
"SECS patient support and help at right time being the motivating factor to access more services"
"Reliable Transportation as a need to continue services further"
"Thought there isn't anything could help with her situation"
"Have saved the website link in Email"
Sub-theme 4.8: Information Delay Due to Information Gap
Description: Users discover resources late, often after prolonged need, because information about available services is not proactively distributed or easily discoverable.
"Would have used pantry services sooner had she known"
"Many resources out there but you have to find them"
"Flyers at different places needed to distribute information"
Sub-theme 4.9: Don't Know What They Need
Description: Users struggle to articulate their needs or understand how services map to their goals, suggesting a gap in need-assessment support or service navigation guidance.
"Don't know what they exactly want from services"
Description: Psychological barriers around shame and stigma prevent engagement with pantries and associated services, even when need exists.

The Awareness-Interest Gap: Users fall into distinct stages: Not Aware → Aware but No Time → Aware but No Path. Interventions must target the specific stage.
Structural Time Poverty: The "Working Hungry" are the most likely to benefit from career services but the least likely to have time to access them.
First Impressions: "First experience" determines long-term engagement. If the first interaction is confusing, they won't return for non-food services.
What do the pantry users desire from the pantry?
Definition: While users prioritize immediate relief, their underlying desires focus on long-term advancement, employment, and financial self-sufficiency.
Increase income is needed to pay bills

Suggestion: SECS should take into account the mindset and needs of users when conveying messages through various channels, including the website and online platforms. Carefully crafted messaging and thoughtfully designed information are essential for effective communication.
Definition: Specific needs related to overcoming language barriers to access broader opportunities.
SECS Evidence: Motivated to access services to learn English, requests more Spanish support
Accessible Learning Tools (e.g., Wants free tools/resources to learn English)
Subtheme 5.3: Material Needs Beyond Basic Food
Definition: Requirements for essential non-food items and specific health-related resources that standard food pantries may overlook.
Household Essentials (e.g., Cleaning supplies needed, depends/adult diapers needed for elderly, clothes and shoes provided)
Other Evidence: Ingredient substitutes needed for health reasons
Definition: The desired "texture" of the interaction—how users want to be treated and how they want services delivered.
SECS Evidence:  "Warm, Low-Pressure Support Feels Safest," preferred roles: Helpful Neighbor/Caring Friend, support that doesn't feel pushy)
SECS Evidence:  Wrote their names, want to be identified personally
Want clear explanation of the financial service,
1. Hierarchy of Needs: "Money is priority." Educational goals are secondary unless they lead directly to income. Long-term "general education" is a hard sell compared to immediate income support.

2. The "Path to Stability" Mindset: Contrary to the view of pantry users as passive recipients of aid, the data shows a strong drive for upward mobility. Users are asking for tools to fix the root cause (income/skills) rather than just the symptom (hunger).
3. The "Low-Pressure" Paradox: Users want "low-pressure" support (no surveillance) but also want to be "identified personally" (relationship).

4. Language as a Gateway: The explicit "motivation to access services to learn English" identifies language not just as a communication preference, but as a desired service outcome. Users view language acquisition as a key resource the community hub can provide to unlock other opportunities.
Recommendations: designed information/messages that cater to neighbors’ needs (framework in the insights)
What are the physical/mental challenges the pantry users face?
Definition: Chronic conditions and disabilities that limit employment and mobility.
"They expect me to do things I'm not physically capable to do"
"Needs more veggies as part of diet (diabetes)"
SECS Evidence: Users want to work (often part-time) but are restricted by heavy duties caring for parents or children.
Definition: Psychological barriers including anxiety, trauma, and depression that prevent engagement.
"Can't work due to mental health or anxiety"
Definition: Social shame and fear of judgment that leads to avoidance behavior.
"Does not like to ask for help (beyond food)"
Definition: Systemic gaps in government support that trap users in poverty.
"Needed food assistance due to Food Stamp Ineligibility"
The Cascade Effect: Challenges are not isolated. A health crisis leads to job loss, which leads to housing instability, which leads to mental health decline.
The "Caregiving Trap" Immobilizes the Workforce The data shows a distinct group who want to work ("wants part-time work") but are physically stuck at home caring for others
Stigma as an Access Barrier: "Pride" and "Avoidance" prevent users from accessing services even when they qualify.
Policy Gaps: The "Working Hungry" often fall into the gap. For example, they earn too much for SNAP but too little to survive.
What are the things pantry users want to achieve in the future?
Definition: The tangible assets and financial states required to feel secure, functioning as the baseline for the "best self."
Hope to find a home for family
Having own house and car as a stable and happy self
SECS Evidence: Hopes to have some income predictability and budgeting, wants to be financially stable
SECS Evidence: Having more money for a car, transportation stability
Definition: Aspirations centered on the user’s role as a provider, where personal success is defined by the stability and future of their children/family.
Better future for their kids being the motivation to keep going
Aspiring to work more so they can help their family
SECS Evidence: Wants better living situation and stability, hopes hard times will improve)
Definition: The desire for self-improvement, education, and the pursuit of personal interests.
Having confidence to approach job because of having right education
Finished education to pursue career in nursing
SECS Evidence:  Would like art activities, would like to go fishing, wants to try bingo if nothing was holding them back, aspires to crochet)
Todo: need to reframe the statements focused on conversation, how SECs can respond to these tensions

Suggestion: Develop a clear pathway that links education to career support, addressing any gaps and providing transitional assistance. This comprehensive framework should facilitate connections between individuals at various transitional points and the resources they need for their next steps.
Definition: The ultimate stage of the aspiration journey where the user transitions from a recipient of help to a provider of help.
SECS Evidence:  Help youngsters build businesses, story sharing/support back

1. The Journey from "Sustenance" to "Giving Back": The diagram at the top of your board perfectly visualizes the user's ideal trajectory: Sustenance → Stability/Autonomy → Growth → Support. Users do not view themselves as permanent dependents. Their "best self" is explicitly defined as someone who has stabilized their own life enough to "help youngsters" or "give back to the community."
Suggestion: Are there current initiatives in place to engage alumni who might be interested in contributing through volunteering, ambassadorship, or mentorship opportunities?

2. Stability is a Family Project, Not an Individual One: The motivation for stability is rarely framed as "I want to be rich." It is almost exclusively framed as "better future for their kids" or "help their family". This suggests that interventions (like AV transport or job coaching) should be marketed as tools for family legacy rather than just individual career advancement.

3. Aspirations for life quality: While housing and finance are expected goals, the specific mentions of activities are profound. In poverty, leisure is often treated as a luxury one cannot afford; expressing a desire for it is an assertion of identity and humanity beyond survival mode.

One liner: Mobility for Stability
SECS Identity: Working family services, suggestion: Offer activities people can enjoy during their difficult time 
curating experiences within the established community, space for energy and recreation to maintain their life.
What are the things in pantry user’s life that keeps them moving forward positively?

Description: Family, especially children are the most powerful motivator for persistence, hard work, and positive change. Parental identity and desire to provide for/protect family sustains effort through crisis.
"Blended family. Kids on both sides and adopted kids. Dealt with custody battles to adopt the 2 kids (niece and nephew)"
"Their kid being the motivation to survive"
"Love from their family helps them to keep going when things are tough"
"Friends family and god helps them keep going when things feel tough"
Description: Religious faith and spiritual practice as source of strength, hope, and emotional grounding during hardship, providing meaning and resilience.
"Spirit of Jesus and impact of people keeps neighbor going during tough times"
[Note: "Friends family and god helps them keep going" combines family + faith motivators]
Description: Personal interests, creative outlets, and leisure activities that provide joy, identity, and purpose beyond survival, representing a full personhood.
"Fiancé likes to bake as a hobby"
"User has many hobbies: sculpting, drawing, blacksmithing, leather work and metalsmithing"
Description: Sense of connection to community and belonging to social networks that provide support and meaning.
Description: Internal drive, determination, and will to survive and persist—intrinsic motivation not dependent on external relationships.
"Will to live makes them keep going"
"Receiving Mode": Outreach is most effective when users are in their natural motivational environments—Faith (Church), Family (School events), or Hobbies (Workshops).
Hobbies as Personhood: Creative pursuits reveal that users retain a strong sense of identity. Services should leverage these skills (e.g., skill-sharing workshops).
What do the pantry users have to say about the pantry? What is their experience?
Definition: Aspects of the pantry experience that users praise and value.
"Neighbors mentioned SECS staff are very kind to everyone"
"Order on Pantry soft website is simple"
"Food is ready, you just pull up... so it's easy"
"Not able to get all they need to cook ideal meal"
"Beech Grove Pantry does not hand out meat and there is a raffle ticket system"
Definition: Rules or physical constraints that create barriers.
"Person needs to be present to get pantry items"
Human Connection is the "Sticky" Factor: Users remain loyal for years despite supply gaps because of the Staff Kindness and lack of discrimination.
Operational Excellence: SECS's drive-through and app-based ordering are major strengths compared to "Others," solving the "Long Waits" and "Confusion" seen elsewhere.
Definition: Feedback on the automated interview process, ranging from technical glitches to privacy concerns.
"AI end the interview but the participants have not finished talking"
"Issue with the interview as children are noise"
"Is not sure if someone will listen to the conversation or not"
"Describes AI interview as good and understandable"
"Colors of markers brought memories of late husband"
